utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has decided that it's better to complete this witness first and then go back to the submissions on the documents as indicated earlier. So we continue with cross-examination, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Can the witness be given P124 again, please. Cross-examined by Mr. Di Fazio: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mirkic, I'd like you to have a look at point 13 in the gazette, in fact, the same part of the document that I was asking you about yesterday. It's dealing with a supposed meeting of the Executive Board on the 14th of April, 1992. It contains the six conclusions. This meeting -- the entry is dated the 14th of April, 1992, signed by Mirko Jovanovic. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In point 3, there's a reference to the assigning to the chief of the public security station, who is Stevan Todorovic, the task of immediately forming a special purposes unit of the MUP, attached to the SJB, the public security station, in collaboration with the responsible bodies of the military and civilian authorities. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in that body? How many members did it have?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where it was housed, where it had its headquarters or office?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it ever discussed at Executive Board meetings?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of its existence?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you explain? The existence of what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This special purposes unit of the MUP, attached to the SJB, the public security station, which is to collaborate with responsible bodies of the military and civilian authorities. Are you aware of its existence?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever attend any meetings of the Executive Board at which Stevan Todorovic was present?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of his ever having attended Executive Board meetings?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was never with me at any of the Executive Board meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever send any subordinates to Executive Board meetings?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I knew very few of these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You sent representatives occasionally to Executive Board meetings, didn't you, representatives of the secretariat for the economy?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was very often Milan Simic who attended Executive Board meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your instructions?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was according to a previous agreement. That's why he often represented this secretariat. This was based on a verbal agreement with President Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the situation with your membership of the Executive Board was not only were you an unqualified economist, not having any knowledge of the social and political scenario in the municipality, you actually didn't attend many meetings of the Executive Board as well.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend many of the meetings of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of work did you do?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise in your question? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: Did you have to undergo a period of training in order to acquaint yourself with the political and social conditions that applied in Bosanski Samac in April and May, so that -- in order to be able to carry out these duties that had been thrust upon you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have to go -- undergo anything, and my duties were of day-to-day nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I may have asked this yesterday. I apologise if I'm repeating myself. But did you actually attend any Executive Board meetings in person?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many did you attend?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six or seven maybe, but I can't give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on those occasions, were there any police representatives at all that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mirkic, one of the decisions in that document that you have before you - I needn't trouble you to find it in the document itself - lists the decision made on the 28th of March, 1992, on the election of various members of the Executive Council, or Executive Board, and you're second on the list as secretary of the municipal secretariat for the economy. One of the other appointees is a gentleman named Mico Ivanovic, commander of the Territorial Defence municipal staff. Do you know that man?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Maybe for the sake of fairness, it is at page 7 of B/C/S version, which is in front of -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'm grateful to Mr. Pantelic for that. Thank you. I didn't actually know the B/C/S page number and I was hoping to avoid delay and I'm grateful to Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As Mr. Pantelic points out, Mr. Mirkic, you'll find it at page 7, so you can read it for yourself. Can you turn to page 7?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Pantelic. I think the counsel has picked it up. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you see this fellow's name about halfway down the list, Mico Ivanovic, commander of the Territorial Defence. Do you know this man?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know this man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you knew that he was a member of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision was never implemented to the full.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What parts of it weren't implemented? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirko Jovanovic, Lazar Mirkic, Mirko Lukic, and Dragomir Tesanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about them?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the people who worked in the Executive Board and whom I used to see there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. And is it the absence of the others on the six occasions that you did attend meetings lead you to the conclusion that they were not involved?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were probably connected with the relevant state ministries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you straight out: Obviously Todorovic is not one of the people you say who worked in the Executive Board. Are you saying that he was never a member of the Executive Board pursuant to this decision? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw him at Executive Board meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it that that makes you tell this Chamber that therefore he was not a member of the Executive Board or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was not a member of the Executive Board, because he did not report about his work to the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And two of the people whose name you haven't mentioned as working at the Executive Board, people who did not work or function at the Executive Board, were Milos Bogdanovic and Bozo Ninkovic, and they're both representatives of National Defence, as you can see in the document. Is it the case, are you saying that National Defence had no representation on the Executive Board? Never turned up, didn't attend meetings, didn't send representatives, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they did not have anything whatsoever to do with the Executive Board. They also did not report to the Executive Board about their work. They were not responsible to the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the use of labour under the work obligation programme? That was a matter that was dealt with by the Executive Board, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was a matter that was under the jurisdiction or a matter that was within the area of responsibility of National Defence, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we asked from the National Defence was to -- as regards persons who were required to be at certain places under their work obligation, to relieve them of their duties in the army, i.e., in the areas that this secretariat for National Defence was responsible for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you required people to work pursuant to the work obligation in all sorts of areas: On farms, factories, and so on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In companies. They were directors who came up with a possible organisation and requirements for labour, and then they would turn to the municipal secretariat for National Defence and they would ask for their approval, to give them the people that they needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was an ongoing phenomenon, wasn't it? The needs for workers, the need for workers was continuing, constant demands?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Often times the situation changed. During season, companies would require more people and then when they did not need as many workers, those people would go back to the places from which they had been taken from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to the man I asked you about originally in that list of elected members of the Executive Board, Mico Ivanovic. Now, you say he didn't attend any meetings of the Executive Board. Did you know him to be the commander of the Territorial Defence, municipal staff, as it says in the document?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know what duties Mico discharged. I had known him, as he was previously employed in Orasje, and that's how I got to know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the 16th and 17th of April, what precisely was the Territorial Defence in Bosanski Samac, in the town of Bosanski Samac, TO or Territorial Defence? Where was it, who was a member of it, who commanded it, what did it do? And I'm talking about the period of time after the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't be able to answer that question. I don't know. I don't know absolutely anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The six or so meetings that you attended of the Executive Board, they were held in the Municipal Assembly building in Bosanski Samac, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is -- let me withdraw that. Over what period of time did you attend these six or so meetings?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly in June and early July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to the Municipal Assembly or the offices of the Executive Board on other occasions, but perhaps not for meetings but for other business, to consult with your colleagues or whatever?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe once or twice. I mostly did other things while I was attending those meetings, so whatever other things I had to do, I would do before or after the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean things in Bosanski Samac, matters you had to attend to in the town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not only in Bosanski Samac, but in the whole general area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What I'm interested in is your visits to the offices of the Executive Board in the municipal building. This is the situation, as I understand it: You went there on about six or so occasions to attend formal meetings, plus you may have gone there on two or so occasions for other business, not being meetings. That's so, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These were visits during the day?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Municipal Assembly building is right next door to the SUP building and not very far away at all from the TO building; that is so, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any sounds coming from the SUP building or the TO building on your visits there to the Municipal Assembly building? Sorry?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't hear any screams, yells of tortured men, nothing like that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear any choruses singing Chetnik songs? Did you ever hear that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On those occasions that you did attend the municipal building, did you ever see any of the defendants present, Mr. Blagoje Simic, Dr. Blagoje Simic, Mr. Tadic, possibly Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the meetings take at the Executive Board on those six or so occasions that you attended them?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were mostly short meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you have -- MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be given his statement, his 92 bis statement, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can I ask you to look at paragraph 17, and in fact the last sentence of that paragraph. Just re-read it. Okay. Now, you say there that part of the population of Samac municipality, plus a large number of Serbian refugees, were put up at Zasavica for security reasons; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of these people were indeed accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't understand your answer. The way I read your statement -- you tell me if I'm correct. That's what I want to know. The way I read your statement, you were saying two groups of people were put in Zasavica. Part of the population of Samac, one group; Serbian refugees, a second group; and both groups were put there for security reasons. Is that what in fact you were saying in your statement?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any reliable information as to who exactly was there, but that was what rumour had, and that is that Serbian refugees from other parts of Bosnia who were on their way towards Samac, and some of the local population were put there for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So this part in your statement, in your Rule 92 bis statement, is based on rumour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you include rumour in your statement? Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That's a problem with the interpretation, with the translation. This witness said that he heard this fact from the other people, and wrong interpretation in terms of rumour came to the earphones of my learned friend. So it's hearsay, to be precise. It's hearsay. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: That's my idea of rumour, but in any event, we won't split hairs over --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: -- Over --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No. To be honest, and to be fair with this witness, he said that he heard this fact from the other persons. He never mentioned rumours in B/C/S. So please be fair. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand what Mr. Pantelic is saying. I won't use the word again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That part of your statement is based purely on what you heard from other people?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other people?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't specify what other people, but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you can't remember who you heard it from, you don't know with what authority they spoke on the subject, you can't remember how many people you spoke to about the subject, you can't remember when you spoke to people about the subject, but you're quite happy to put it into your statement. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my earlier statements before this Tribunal, I did say that I had spent very little time in Samac and that I only knew very few people over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know. I heard that.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it is for these reasons that I cannot be any more specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I heard your evidence very clearly. You made that quite clear, Mr. Mirkic, and it's precisely that, it's precisely that lack of knowledge, your lack of knowledge, that should have prevented you from putting in these -- such assertions; don't you agree?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what you're asking me to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you this: You mention in that part of your statement part of the population of Samac municipality. Based on what you heard from other people, what part of the population did you know or did you understand had been taken to Zasavica? The population of Samac. I'm not talking about the Serb refugees.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the structure of that population. I don't know who was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never heard that it was Croats who were taken to Zasavica? You never heard that from your contacts that you've told us about?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were members of all ethnic groups there, from what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the part of the population of Samac municipality. I'm quoting directly from your statement: "The part of the population of Samac municipality." That part, do you have any information as to their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement, I stated that part of the population of Samac municipality, as well as many refugees, were there, but I did not know what their ethnicity was. I assume that members of all ethnic groups were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. And you mention these people being put up in Zasavica for security reasons. Now, what did you hear were the security reasons for their accommodation in Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the fact that there was less shelling over there, because Samac was being shelled on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's something that you also heard from these undefined people in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had occasion to see this for myself several times when I was there, that Samac was indeed being shelled. I'm talking about the few times that I was actually there. I fled from Samac myself, as fast as I could, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is this -- what I'm asking you is this: In paragraph 17, you say that these people were put up there for security reasons, put up in Zasavica. Now, I'm not disputing that Samac was shelled. I know about that. What I'm asking you is: Please tell the Trial Chamber what you understood the security reasons to be.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've said --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. To be fair -- I'm sorry. I don't want to misunderstand you. Are you saying that because you saw Bosanski Samac being shelled, that you concluded that that's the reason people were taken to Zasavica? Is that fair? So that they would be safer?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't -- I was not the one who was in charge of security. Someone else was in charge of that. Therefore, I can't give you a clear answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you can't give me a clear answer, why did you include it in your statement? I mean, this is a statement that's going to be read by these Judges and they have to draw factual conclusions. You've just told us you can't be clear about why the people were taken to Zasavica, but in your statement you're quite clear. You say for security reasons. Now, why did you make that assertion if you can't be clear?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably I based my statement or assertion on ideas that I had, that all the villages and the surroundings were much safer than the town of Samac itself. So it was actually a loose remark that I included in my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And how many other loose remarks are there in the statement that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't -- I didn't keep track.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, in evidence, in answer to questions from Mr. Pantelic, you said that there was no form of ethnic discrimination in Bosanski Samac; quite the contrary. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant institutionalised discrimination, that kind of thing. Now, as to whether there were individuals who committed certain acts, what those acts were that they perhaps committed, now that's a different issue altogether. What I had in mind, above all, was that no official institution ever publicly favoured ethnic or any other kind of discrimination among the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're aware, aren't you, that following April 16 and 17, large-scale arrests of Croats and Muslims took place in Bosanski Samac? You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. You didn't know that there were Croats and Muslims being imprisoned in the SUP, in the TO building, in the high school gym, in the primary school gym? You didn't know about that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of it since, that phenomenon happening since April -- or since 1992, in effect?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear about it. People were talking about it, that that was indeed what had happened. But at that time, I was really not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. You're aware that the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac that was proclaimed or declared after the 16th of April only permitted Serbian representatives, people of Serbian ethnicity, amongst its ranks? You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there was an opening for other ethnic groups, citizens of other ethnic groups to take part in the work of the authorities and in the bodies of government, but I was not personally involved in the setting up of these bodies, of these authorities. Therefore, I can't provide a more specific answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what makes you believe that there was an opening for other ethnic groups in the new institutions of the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac? Why is it that you say that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have based this statement on my personal views and understanding. I never once heard that anyone had actually banned them from taking part in the authorities in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're aware of names and -- names of streets, locations in Bosanski Samac and the municipality itself being changed in order to fit -- in order to remove names associated with the history of the Muslim and ethnic communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not while I was there. No such thing happened while I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of large numbers of Muslims and Croats leaving the municipality of Bosanski Samac and the town of Bosanski Samac through a programme called the Exchange Programme? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was happening throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was something that -- excuse me. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do. I don't want to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this was something that was generally accepted by all the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, informing us of that. Now, can you tell us: Are you aware of large numbers of Muslims and Croats leaving the municipality of Bosanski Samac and the town of Bosanski Samac through a programme called the Exchange Programme, or exchanges?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them did indeed leave, but some of them stayed in Samac until the very end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see them being loaded onto buses carrying their belongings in suitcases and so on? Did you ever see that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never personally witnessed any of these exchanges or people getting ready to leave and be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your assistance. MR. DI FAZIO: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Pantelic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mirkic, you were asked by the Prosecutor about work obligations that people had, and in reply to that question, you said there was a certain principle and that the whole thing was based on a number of regulations. My question is: Which ethnic groups or nationalities did the work obligation apply to?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This applied to the whole population, or rather, all those individuals who had not been mobilised, drafted, into the ranks of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the whole population, please state the ethnic groups you have in mind, for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs, Croats, Muslims, and the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I don't have further questions for the witness. [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Mirkic. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Mirkic. I just have a couple of questions for you based on your testimony yesterday and this morning. I'd like to know whether your appointment as secretary for economy in the executive committee of Samac municipality was formalised by a decision of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not by a decision of the Crisis Staff. It was a decision by the Assembly, the Assembly held on the 28th of March, 1992. However, this decision became effective after the 17th of April, came into effect after the 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Secondly, you were asked a few questions by the Prosecutor concerning paragraph 17 of your statement concerning the village of Zasavica, and I'm wondering: Was the situation in Zasavica ever discussed at the Executive Board meetings that you attended?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thirdly, you mentioned, in response to the Prosecutor, that your mentioning of Zasavica in paragraph 17 of your statement, you said, was actually a loose remark. What I'm wondering is: Why did you, in this remark, refer only to Zasavica and not to the other villages in the surroundings of the town of Bosanski Samac which you mention on page 13, line 22 and 23? Why did you single out Zasavica to make this remark in paragraph 17?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was probably the village was near the town of Samac, and it was relatively safe, so people could be accommodated there, at least for a brief period of time, until such time as the whole thing stopped. We all hoped that it would stop soon, that the conflict would soon be over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question concerns a meeting that took place at Agroposavina on 12th of April, 1992. Agroposavina was your workplace? Am I correct in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So I'm wondering whether you were present at this meeting at Donji Zabar, at Agroposavina, on 12th of April, 1992. Can you recall being present at a meeting on that date?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's been a long time and I can't say the date rings any bells. I can't recall that specific date, I'm afraid, or what meeting may have been held on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If I said to you it was a meeting concerning a number of men who had arrived by helicopter a little bit earlier in Batkusa, would that refresh your memory? Can you recall a meeting that took place at your workplace in Agroposavina and was attended by persons from Bosanski Samac? If you can't recall it, you know, simply say you can't recall it.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that no such meetings were ever actually held at Agroposavina. I did not take part in any such meeting. I was away on business quite often, so it's possible that I was not even there on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just want to seek clarification from you on the terms that you have used in your statement, because in the other pieces of evidence, the terms are different. When you talk of the executive committee, is that the same thing as the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may be a typo, because all we ever speak about is the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. We are finished with your evidence. Thank you very much for coming. You are now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, would it be appropriate time for me to tender one of these redacted versions of the previous statements or we shall proceed with the witness and at a later stage we shall deal with the procedural matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. We are supposed to have submissions on the exhibits tendered by Mr. Lukic and the Prosecution regarding the International Red Cross agreements on exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours; good morning to all participants. My understanding of the ruling of the Trial Chamber is that we should briefly explain why both we ourselves and the Office of the Prosecutor have tendered these documents into evidence. So now the Trial Chamber would like to have our brief submissions. I will try to keep it as brief as possible, speaking on behalf of Mr. Tadic's Defence. Your Honours, the Office of the Prosecutor, when speaking about the exchanges, has made several claims about things that we could see summed up in the last questions that Mr. Di Fazio addressed to the witness. The term he was using was the Exchange Programme, and he claims this is one of the elements of persecution. In paragraph 2 of the indictment, the Office of the Prosecutor claimed the same thing when giving the general information concerning Mr. Tadic; these claims were elaborated in the pre-trial brief item 25. Their views on these exchanges were also elaborated when introducing exchange lists at the end of their case, and the Prosecutor's understanding of these exchanges was also indicated by the questions they asked numerous witnesses and the report of the special envoy of the UN, Mr. Mazowiecki on ethnic cleansing. There was word of exchanges taking place occasionally there also. The documents that we have proposed and the documents tendered by the Prosecutor seem to indicate something that seems to be an agreed fact. Both parties obviously agree for these documents to be introduced, but obviously both parties have their own different interpretation of these documents. I must try hard not to go into that right now, not to go into evaluating the actual evidence. So what I'm going to say is that Mr. Tadic's Defence, if I may remind you, in our opening brief, promised to prove that the exchanges were no invention of the Samac committee of the town of Samac or of Miroslav Tadic. I said we would prove that these exchanges were carried out in a number of different ways, but in the ways that we have tried to prove and across a wider area, not only Posavina, Republika Srpska, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, but rather, in the area of the entire former Yugoslavia; and thirdly, that international institutions actively participated in these exchanges, regardless if, as observers, organisers, or supervisors. I think this has been agreed in this trial that all the exchanges that took place in the UNPA zones, Dragalic and Lipovac, were indeed witnessed tendered by representatives of the UNPROFOR, and on the other hand that a large number of exchanges was being attended by representatives of the international humanitarian organisations, particularly the Red Cross. The logic inherent in this, the Defence of Mr. Tadic, led us to tender into evidence the documents that we offered at the end of our case. I merely wish to point out that we informed the Prosecution about these documents during reciprocal disclosure prior to the beginning of the trial itself. We did disclose a number of documents during the Prosecution case, but it was prior to the commencement of the trial that the Prosecution already had all the documents that we were then tendering. Briefly, in relation to document D190, agreement number 2, upon the invitation of the International Red Cross, dated the 23rd of May, 1992, this agreement between the warring sides or parties, paragraph 2 refers to the work of the commission and the persons to work on the exchanges and the lists of detained persons. Document D191/3, the proposal by UNPROFOR for a reciprocal release of detainees, adopted prior to the 9th of December, 1992, shows that the Defence is right in claiming that UNPROFOR also had a notable role to play in these exchanges and in liberating detained persons by way of this exchange programme. Paragraph 3 says that the essence of the whole idea of the exchanges is what is in paragraph 7 too, and something we have been trying to prove before this Tribunal, that these exchanges were actually a humanitarian and above all humane act. I will remind you that I said at the beginning that Mr. Tadic's Defence will try to prove that these exchanges were not part of restricting human rights, which is an indispensable element of the actus reus, but rather that the exchanges were a way to see these human rights implemented. Following that, another document marked D192/3, conclusions, dated 16th December 1992, agreed between the Republic of Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. These seem to indicate that further exchanges had taken place between two institutions which are not directly involved in our case, but this clearly indicates and proves right the assertion by the Defence that the exchanges indeed took place throughout the former Yugoslavia. And what I found particularly note worthy is that in this agreement, again you have Lipovac and Dragalic as locations where the exchanges were to be carried out, for the obvious reason that those were the safest possible locations at that time. Another document which we tendered into evidence which was marked D193/3 is a document of the International Red Cross, describing the procedure applied during the exchanges, document dated June 1993. In our view, this shows the existence of the very procedure which existed in relation to the lists of persons to be exchanged and the checking of those lists, as proposed by the International Red Cross as early as June 1993. In point of fact, it was precisely those principles that people actually worked on the exchanges, both those from Samac and those that they were cooperating with applied, and eventually document that was marked D194/3, an extract from the Paris Peace Agreement, specifically Article 9, which seems to me essential because it shows that civilians and military personnel were mentioned as equal in that document concerning the exchanges and that both these groups had the same right to be exchanged. That's as far as our documents are concerned, the documents tendered by us. As far as the documents tendered by the Office of the Prosecutor are concerned, as I said, I have no general objections, because these documents refer to the same issue. So personally, I believe that document marked as P179, again guidelines provided by the International Red Cross, dated 24th of March, 1993, I believe that these guidelines are almost identical to the document that I spoke about now, D193, also containing guidelines but from June 1993. In relation to the document marked P178, the agreement between the warring parties, dated the 13th of September and 1st of October, 1992, I believe, as far as Article 3, paragraph 6 is concerned of this particular document, and Article 9, this document again describes the exchanges, the right of the people to take sides and the right of the people to choose freedom of movement. I think this is merely a supplement to the same set of documents that we shall address in our final brief more specifically. Document P176 is in fact the first introductory part of another document, an agreement, dated the 22nd of May, 1992, between the warring parties, which is actually the first part of the document that we tendered as document 190/3. I did have this document, and it's quite possible that I served this document on the Prosecutor during reciprocal disclosure. I think this is a relevant document because it speaks about the status of detainees, and practically binds the signatories in terms of the Geneva Conventions and the status of the civilian population and detainees. I think this is a very relevant document, because it in no way refers to the exchanges themselves as actually carried out. I think it's a legal point now, a point of legal interpretation, whether this document is relevant for my case. But as it is an integral part of a document that I have tendered, I have no objection to this document being introduced, but I think it is irrelevant for us and for what we're trying to prove. Finally, the document that was marked P177, that's what we refer to as agreement number 3, dated June 1992, an agreement between the warring parties. Miroslav Tadic's Defence disclosed this document to the Office of the Prosecutor, but after further verification and in terms of our case, the case we're trying to prove through these documents, this document has appeared to me irrelevant because it speaks about making it possible for representatives of the International Red Cross to actually provide assistance, which was their task. However, page 8 of this document speaks about the separation of families and the need for the International Red Cross to organise some sort of a search service, searching for missing persons, everything that we've heard during Mr. Tadic's defence when we spoke about the cooperation between the local and the International Red Cross. So there is no objection on our part for this document to be tendered and accepted into evidence, but it strikes us as irrelevant for our case. Therefore, on the basis of all these documents, the Defence of Mr. Miroslav Tadic believes that we have proven that the way the exchanges took place and how the Samac committee worked can by no means be reduced to what the Prosecution has claimed. On the contrary, the exchanges carried out by the Samac commission and all the institutions it cooperated with were carried out fully, in accordance with the principles -- the international principles and the human rights. We shall try to use these documents once again to show that this principle was indeed applied and that the exchanges were carried out during the period of the indictment throughout the former Yugoslavia; and secondly, that the international organisations did take active part in observing, supervising, and organising these exchanges, in assisting these exchanges, providing all necessary assistance for the basic human rights and entitlements to be implemented. I'm not sure whether a reply to this will be, but this for the time being is our position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, the Prosecution. Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution understands fully Mr. Lukic's submission in relation to the relevance of the documents he has tendered to his client's case, and we certainly don't oppose them. Your Honours will recall the evidence you heard from the local Red Cross representative, Mr. Maslic, and indeed Mr. Tadic himself, as to the role of the ICRC in the exchanges as they have been called before this Trial Chamber. Mr. Maslic's evidence was of the International Red Cross brokering and organising the first exchange in May 1992. That was evidence he gave earlier, on January 11th, 12th -- sorry - 10th, 11th, and 14th of this year. Mr. Tadic himself, in his re-examination by Mr. Lukic, at page 15.793, said: "All those who refused to be exchanged went home. That was the results of the first exchange ever, ever," meaning back in May 1992, "when the ICRC informed me" -- sorry - "informed us of this obligation and we complied with it to the letter." The Prosecution -- that's the end of the quote. The Prosecution is anxious to ensure that the Trial Chamber has the complete picture in relation to the ICRC's involvement, if at all, in the -- what has been term euphemistically the exchange process. The Defence of Mr. Tadic has tendered two documents which, if taken in isolation, give -- can be give a misleading impression or picture of what the ICRC was actually doing during the indictment period. As Your Honours, of course, are aware, the effect of the Appeal Chamber's ruling prevented the Prosecution from calling direct evidence from a former Red Cross casual employee. So the Prosecution did not call any evidence during its case in relation to the ICRC. However, these documents are all public documents which have become relevant once the Defence has put them into evidence or has used the ICRC as part of its case to justify the role of Mr. Tadic and the Exchange Commission in a sense that it was complying at all times with the ICRC guidelines. Agreements between the warring parties and international humanitarian law. The two documents which Mr. Lukic tendered, specific ICRC documents, as I mentioned a moment ago, if taken together, would give a misleading picture that the exchange process may have been something the ICRC was condoning or participating in. However, you have to see the other documents. The first document was D190/3, which is an agreement or -- it's actually the setting up of the commission, but pursuant to an agreement of the 22nd of May, 1992. Now, the parties to the agreement, which is in P176, which the Prosecution tendered, are quite important, because the parties are the representative of Mr. Izetbegovic, the president of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; a representative of Mr. Karadzic, the president of the SDS; and a representative of the HVO, or the Croatian Democratic Community, I'm sorry. Those, of course, were the warring parties in the indictment period, in the indictment geographical area. But more importantly, Your Honour has heard a lot of evidence of the role of the SDS, of which, of course, Mr. Karadzic was the leader during the indictment period, and he was in fact at the time of the signing of these agreements and all subsequent ones the president of the presidency of the Republika Srpska. Your Honours have heard an abundance of evidence, most recently a few days ago, from Mr. Mitar Mitrovic, the secretary of the Municipal Assembly and the Crisis Staff, that the municipal bodies, the Serbian Samac municipality, the Executive Council or Executive Board, and so on, were bound to follow government policies, government decrees, government regulations. This is an agreement, or these were a series of agreements signed by a representative of the government. That's President Karadzic. Whose decrees, regulations, and laws they were obliged to follow. Now, the agreement of -- P176 is particularly relevant in response to the Defence tender, because it's an agreement as to the civilian population. Specifically, Article 2.3 on page 3 refers to -- in terms -- of course in terms of the 4th Geneva Convention. I'm not going to go into the Geneva Conventions or anything, but it refers specifically to an agreement between the parties and a special agreement that they are bound to honour the provisions of Geneva 4, and specifically sets out in the treatment -- "in the treatment of the civilian population, there should be no adverse distinction founded on race, religion, or faith or any other similar criteria and the displacement of the civilian population shall not be ordered unless the security of the civilian is involved or imperative military reasons so demand." That's in Article 2.3 of the special agreement of that document. And Your Honours must see P176 if Your Honours are to see D193, which D190/3 is merely an agreement made pursuant to set up a commission made pursuant to this initial agreement on the 22nd of May, 1992. The next one, of course, is D -- sorry - P177. That's the 6th of June agreement in Geneva. Again it's the same parties, and I do note, and accept my learned friend Mr. Lukic's submissions as to the relevance of this particular document, and I do concede it is the least relevant of the ICRC documents. It has been tendered to complete the picture, so to speak, of agreements 1, 2, 3, and 4, so that Your Honours have a complete picture of the agreements between the warring parties and the application to the civilian population in any particular municipality or any part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There are two particularly relevant portions in it, that's at page 8 and pages 9 of the agreement number 3 under the heading number 4, IV, other ICRC activities page 8 Heading Access to Prisoners, underlined "Access to Prisoners and Visitors to Places Detention Are a Fundamental Part of the ICRC's Mandate. It is imperative that the ICRC gain access to all places of detention under the control of all the parties," it goes on: "ICRC delegates will have free access to all persons captured and detained." And other the page general provisions 5 it mentions as one of the following places Odzak, which is of course one of the municipalities, the subject of the indictment. The next one is P178, which is a very important agreement, if Your Honours are to see the complete picture in relation to Mr. Tadic's case of the exchanges, and I understand of course Dr. Simic's and Mr. Zaric's case as well. And this agreement is called the Geneva Agreement, what's known as the Geneva Agreement. The agreement is headed -- now, this is very important, the agreement is actually headed "Agreement on the Release and Transfer of Prisoners." It's not headed release -- Agreement on the Exchange of Prisoners. It's "Release and Transfer of Prisoners." And the date is very important too. It's the 1st of October, 1992, which is midway through the indictment period. Again, the same representatives: Mr. Karadzic, the president of the presidency of the Republika Srpska and the SDS, of course the controlling body of the municipalities, including the one the subject of this indictment. It doesn't talk about -- this agreement doesn't talk about the exchange of prisoners. It doesn't contemplate the exchange of prisoners. It contemplates only the release and transfer of prisoners. Article 3 on page 2 is headed "Release of Prisoners." Subparagraph 1: "All prisoners not accused of or sentenced to grave breaches of international humanitarian law that is defined in the 4th Geneva Convention," and the additional Protocol I, "will be unilaterally and unconditionally released." II, "each party will release all prisoners it is holding in any given place of detention as soon as the ICRC" -- sorry - "requests on the basis of a specific plan of operation." Article 9 on page 5, notification -- headed "Notification of Releases Without ICRC Involvement," says: "In the event of any release, transfer, repatriation or exchange of prisoners in which the ICRC takes no part, the ICRC will be notified of all the prisoners concerned." That's the only mention of -- that's the only mention of exchange in the whole document. And it is only referring to it in a sense in which the ICRC is not involved, because it does not contemplate the ICRC being involved in exchanges. It is saying the parties agree to notify the ICRC if they have "exchanged prisoners." I won't take Your Honours to international humanitarian law and the exchange of prisoners -- civilian prisoners on a one-to-one basis as opposed to the permissible exchange of prisoners of war, because that's not the situation which pertains to this indictment. Your Honours will note in P178 it refers to some annexures. I neglected, because -- to tender the annexures, I found them this morning under a different ERN number. The annexures actually refer -- one of them refers to the municipality of Bosanski Samac and the detention of prisoners there. That's annexure A. The Prosecution overlooked the reference to the annexures in that, and searching through the system this morning, I located I annexures which had been filed in the system under a different ERN number. It appears that the same document the Geneva agreement has been submitted to the OTP's Evidence Unit on different occasions under different ERN numbers and the one I tendered before did not have the annexure. So I'll come back to that later and I've given a copy to my learned friend this morning when I found the things. Again, they're public documents and the Defence having had these documents, it would cause them no prejudice, because they actually referred to in P178. Which takes me to P179, and this is the first one, dated the 24th of March, 1993, which actually refers to the guidelines for the exchange of prisoners. And it's very important what the introduction says, because if you only go to the document my learned friend Mr. Lukic tendered, which was P193/3, which is a further set of guidelines and principles and procedures for the ICRC involvement, one could get the impression that it is something the ICRC has condoned or been involved in for some period before. It is only -- because this document, of course, doesn't mention the document of the 24th of March, 1993, which is why P179 is so important, and the date is important. It's nine months after the first exchange in Bosanski Samac. That's the exchange Mr. Maslic testified the ICRC actually brokered and organised. And it says in its introduction: "In principle, all prisoners held by the parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina should be immediately and unilaterally released." And refers under the auspices of the Geneva Convention -- the Geneva agreement of the 1st of October. That's P178, and the London agreement of 27th of August, 1992, which was the Vance-Owen Plan. However, "as this obligation has not been fully carried out by the parties, so as not to delay unnecessarily the release of prisoners, international organisations may participate in prisoner exchanges if the following rules are accepted. The aim of these is to humanise the exchanges while attempting to limit their negative side effects." And this is the really important part and why we are tendering this document: "It must be noted that prisoner exchanges were not foreseen by the above-mentioned agreements, and therefore remain the exception to the rule." That's on the 24th of March, 1993, the ICRC is saying prisoner exchanges were not contemplated by the earlier agreements, which places it well after the period in which Mr. Maslic and Mr. Tadic have testified that the ICRC was participating in prisoner exchanges, and it defines prisoners as "all civilians deprived of their liberty for reasons related to the conflict, including those interned, detained, or subject to assigned residence." Again, that relates directly back to the indictment and the evidence which Defence witnesses have given of the reasons for people being in Zasavica and these exchanges where civilians could line up to leave, which is actually contrary to the agreements as set out between the parties. And the rules applicable, one, "international organisations will not initiate exchanges, will only participate or monitor them if these rules are expected"; and 2, "international organisations will do their ultimate most to ensure that persons other than prisoners will not be exchanged and that persons are not arrested in view of the exchange." The clear evidence in the Defence case of Mr. Tadic, Mr. Masic, and others, is that civilians who were not detained, who were not subject to confinement of their liberty were not interned or subject to assigned residence were arriving for exchange, that's exchange of prisoners on one to one -- exchange of people on a one-to-one basis, which this agreement says will do their utmost to ensure that these people are not exchanged. It's only prisoners. So, Your Honours, in my submission, you have to see the full picture to see it in the context of the Defence case, and the Prosecution's response to the selective tendering of only two of the relevant documents in that. In my submission, they are relevant of course to the Defence case, but the Prosecution should be allowed to respond during the Defence case to give the Defence a chance to respond to those if necessary by the tendering of public documents will complete the full picture of the ICRC's involvement and the international community's -- or international organise organisation's attitude to the exchange process. In my submission, these documents are highly relevant and highly probative and necessary for the Trial Chamber's determination of the Defence case. I make no submissions as to the relevance of the two documents D191/3 and D192/3 which the Defence has tendered. The Prosecution considers them to be of marginal relevance but if the Defence considers them necessary to their case, we don't object to their tender and whatever use they wish to make of them in their case or final submissions. Those are my submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and we've just reached about our time for a break. We'll continue with our witnesses after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Pantelic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Marusic. For the record, can you please tell us your full name, the first name and the last name.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: I'm Branislav Marusic. My first name is Branislav and my last name is Marusic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we speak the same language, after my question, can you make a short pause. This will help the interpreters do their job, and participants will be able to follow your words. You are -- in paragraph 1 of your statement, according to paragraph -- according to 92 bis, you gave us your personal data. However, could you please tell us: In 1991, you were a member of the SDS; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Gracanica you were the president of the municipal board of that party of the SDS; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you stop being the president of the municipal board of the SDS in Gracanica, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: I believe that this was sometime in December of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was your successor? Who became the president of the SDS municipal board after you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: After me, the president of the municipal SDS board of Gracanica was Mr. Djordje Ilic. I believe that he was in that post for a short time, and he was followed by Mr. Bosko Dujkovic. But immediately after me, it was Mr. Djordje Ilic who was the president of the SDS in Gracanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Chamber why you resigned from the post of the president of the municipal board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: Since I was also the president of the Executive Board of Gracanica municipality and I had a very busy schedule, I simply did not have the time to dedicate to party activities. Therefore, I resigned and asked to be replaced by somebody who will have more time than me, and this obviously left me more time for my work in the Executive Board of Gracanica municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You left Gracanica because of some threats. I'm just quoting your statement. Can you explain the nature of those threats?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: I was in Gracanica until the end of April, as far as I can remember. I believe I was there until 25th or 26th of April. Then I received some very serious threats. I was told I had to move out because my life was at stake. Then I took my children and my wife and I moved to my family house in Karanovac, where my mother lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did these threats come from? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: I believe that those threats came from the Green Berets, which were paramilitary Muslim units, and these threats usually came during the night or early hours of the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. What did you do between May 1992 and the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: After May 1992, when I discontinued my activities as the president of the Executive Board in Gracanica municipality, I left for Karanovac where I stayed for a certain time in my family house. After that, I was mobilised and joined the army, that is, the Yugoslav People's Army, and that is where I stayed until the end. I did not have any political function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on, did you become a member of the army of Republika Srpska? You mentioned the Yugoslav People's Army, but that was --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was at the beginning. Later on it became the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your position in the army?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: I was a foot soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Let's go back to the period that you mentioned in the statement and why we called you here to give your testimony. There is a piece of evidence in the court files. It's an excerpt from the minutes of the 1st Assembly of the North Bosnia SAO. We're going to come to that later. Before that, I would like to ask you the following: What were the motives for the foundation of the SAO? That was at the beginning of 1991. What preceded the foundation of this autonomous province?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: Everybody knows what was going on and what turbulences were in places in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the main reason was, I believe it was sometime at the end of November, that was the Assembly that took place in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the end of October, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The end of October. There was an outvoting, and there was a declaration about the separation of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the rest of Yugoslavia, after which the Serbian deputies walked out of that assembly, and it was believed that the vital interests of the Serbian people came under threat at that time. After that, there was, so to say, a Serbian politician started thinking as to how to protect the vital Serbian interests, those deputies that had legitimacy as directed deputies by the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. What do you know about, if you know anything about, the way Croats organised themselves at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: I know that we were always forced to make some moves. The Croatian community in Bosnia had already been established. There was a community in Posavina and in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and a similar thing was organised based on a provision of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and a similar thing was organised as an alliance of municipalities. And based on that, we came up -- some municipalities came up with an initiative to establish an association of municipalities in that part of Bosnia. I can't tell you exactly who were the initiators of this initiative and which municipalities were involved. I was a representative of one of those municipalities, municipality of Gracanica. I don't know who the organisers at the local level were. I know that a group of municipalities was involved, and that was a spontaneous meeting which became or turned into the 1st Assembly. I can tell you that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned also some provisions of the constitution or the constitutional framework. Who was it who explained to you and other representatives what those provisions were? Who was it who told you that this was indeed envisaged by the constitution?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: I hope you won't be surprised if I can't answer that. I am a technical person. I am a civil engineer, and I always relied on the professionalism of other people, and that's why I resorted to the opinion of the lawyers who were members of the municipality staff, where they were either presidents of executive boards or presidents of the municipal assemblies. And that's how I learned that this decision did have a foundation in the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that and move to strike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to his opinion as to whether or not the Serbian Autonomous regions have a foundation within the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's outside his knowledge. He's admitted it's outside his knowledge and he indicates he received information from some lawyers, unknown lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's hearsay --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Of an opinion, legal opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He's not discussing the legal issue. He's just explaining he heard what was the basis from the other persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, which is not helpful, actually, Mr. Weiner. The witness has explained about his own knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That he heard that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Simply as that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then, Mr. Marusic. According to these minutes, I can see that Nikola Perisic, a lawyer, was appointed the president of the Assembly of the North Bosnia SAO. Do you know that man?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him. We had some previous meetings within the framework of the intermunicipality cooperation. I know that he was a lawyer and I believe that he had the proper information about the organisation of this association.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he occupy a post at that time, in 1991? You said you were the president of the Executive Board. Was he also occupying some post? If you know.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikola Perisic was the president of municipality in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Let's move on to the analysis of this document, only briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... 10 ter, please. I will repeat. This is Exhibit P10 ter, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you could please just go through it quickly, look at all the pages. I assume you remember this meeting. That was in Doboj, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I remember, and I see that this is an excerpt from the records of that meeting, but I have never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that at that meeting, about 53 out of the total of 61 deputies were present?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I stated in my statement that there were between 50 and 60 deputies present there, but I see here that the exact number was 53, as opposed to the total of 61 who were supposed to be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Marusic, what was the fate of this institution eventually?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: To put it briefly, this was a constitutive meeting of the Assembly and the main bodies were elected. The president, two vice-presidents, and the secretary of the assembly were appointed. After a while, I was appointed president of the government by a group of municipalities, or rather, their representatives and deputies. Northern Bosnia as an autonomous region, practically existed only on paper. It couldn't start operating in practical terms, nor was it involved in anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this Assembly adopt any decision?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: I don't remember any decision being adopted then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this assembly hold meetings or sessions?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I don't think this assembly ever met again, except maybe there was another meeting of several deputies and representatives, the meeting where I was elected president of the government, or rather, nominated. From that point on, I had no further activities there, since I did not have a seat or headquarters. It was supposed to be Doboj, but there were no premises or money to set up a proper working government. And my activities in Gracanica kept unfolding, because I was the president of the Executive Board there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have enough personnel, or rather, people, to fill positions in that government?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: No. There weren't any adequate people or candidates, and there was no money, above all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said that this never really began to function, that it was merely on paper. But other areas, what about other areas and their activity at the time, and what was their relationship to the Northern Bosnia SAO? Can you please explain this to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: My information is that in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were regional organisations based on municipalities, and I believe there were two or three other autonomous regions. I believe Semberija and Majevica. Then there was also Krajina. And if I'm not mistaken, the Romanija region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's outside the scope of our case, so we'll not go any further into that now. The Krajina SAO and the Semberija and Majevica SAO were practically the areas covering this area also?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, in a way. I think the Doboj area was not covered by any of these autonomous regions. Semberija and Majevica, I believe, I heard only later that Samac had joined, based on what initiative I'm not sure, whether initiative was provided by Samac or by someone from Semberija and Majevica for Samac municipality to join. On the other hand, we have Teslic, which was part of the autonomous region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Regarding the appointment or nomination, I mean this one, do you know whether any decisions were actually -- or certificates handed out to people nominated for certain positions? Was this an official thing?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: No. There was no official document handed out to anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on your experience and on your actually being there, physically present, can you please tell the Trial Chamber: What was the gist of this initiative to set up the Northern Bosnia SAO? What was the intention behind that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: If you allow: After my involvement as president of the government who was supposed to set up a functional government and to do something about it, I released -- I gave an interview to Sarajevo TV the next day, and the government, the republican government that was then in place conveyed my statement. I'll repeat this for you. The intention of setting up groups or associations of municipalities was only aimed at preservation, cultural preservation, economic preservation, above all, and in this specific case, what I said about the republican assembly, there was a lot of outvoting and Serbian deputies walked out. To live in that area in an organised manner and for life to be brought back to normal. The intention was not to separate or set aside anyone, Muslims, Croats, or Serbs, and I said this publicly on TV, that this association could hold everyone, all the people, and that no one should try to force their way into it. This was merely for preservation and protection of vital interests, a number of vital interests, economic interests, cultural interests. Of course, there was a certain amount of political involvement at that time too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who prepared the materials for the work of this assembly? Because I see that there was discussion of materials, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: I've never seen those materials. I'm not sure which materials you're talking about. But I think it was all at that meeting, and that assembly meeting, where certain commissions or committees were set up, and they gave -- well, what I think, what I read here, that the secretary was in charge of drawing up an agenda, and no other document or anything like that, in terms of documents, ever came to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without going into further detail, but we're discussing this excerpt from the minutes, there were 53 deputies present. If you turn the page, and if you see that Mr. Nikola Perisic was elected with 32 votes, you are, after all, a man who was involved in politics. You know about majority vote and that kind of thing. You will agree that he was elected by a majority vote?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I assume that this principle of majority or quorum was also applied in the work of the Executive Board, where you worked, and in other political bodies. Was this a principle generally applied?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, if you look just below that, Milovan Milosevic [phoen] or Blagoje Simic, neither of them had garnered the necessary number of votes. What would be your conclusion on the basis of that, as someone who was an insider?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner. That's leading, Mr. Pantelic. You are giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do apologise. I'm asking only about his knowledge of the principles of voting and what his conclusion might be, simple as that. I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You should rephrase your question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore -- I apologise for this interruption, Mr. Marusic. In view of your experience in political bodies, in municipal bodies, tell me, please: When you look at these numbers, at these stats, the results of voting, what would be your conclusion, based on these figures?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, given what the result was of this vote, it is clear that it was the will of the deputies to assign a certain number of votes to each of the candidates, and they were not influenced by anyone. Those who were there and the proposed candidates, what was given here I believe is faithfully conveyed and is a faithful reflection of what really happened at the assembly meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But these two signatories did not have the majority?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV MARUSIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. Why don't you ask the witness to tell what transpired?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
